- Specific supporting fact: In contemporary land-grant charters (copper plates) and epigraphic records such as the Junagadh Inscription of Skandagupta, Vishti (forced labour) is explicitly categorized as an unpaid corvée levy and listed alongside regular taxes (like Bali, Bhaga, and Kara) as an imperial resource or income extracted by the state and delegated to grant-holders.
- Why Option B is incorrect: Inscriptions from the Maitrakas of Valabhi (Kathiawar region) and land grants from central India (Madhya Pradesh) explicitly mention Vishti, confirming it was prevalent rather than absent in these regions.
- Why Option C is incorrect: By definition, Vishti was unfree and unpaid labour demanded by rulers or local landlords; no weekly or periodic wages were provided.
- Why Option D is incorrect: There was no customary or statutory rule specifying that the eldest son had to be sent; labour could be extracted generally from any peasant or artisan household as required.
- Often confused with: 'Begar' in later medieval/colonial times. While both signify unpaid forced labour, ancient Vishti in the Gupta period held formal legal status as an institutionalized tax paid in the form of physical work, rather than an informal feudal imposition.
